newsitem.title: INDIA: Car bomb kills 14 in India's Kashmir.
newsitem.headline: Car bomb kills 14 in India's Kashmir.

text.p: At least 14 people died on Saturday and more than 50 were injured when a powerful car bomb exploded next to a tourist bus in the northern city of Jammu, the leader of India's Jammu and Kashmir state said.

"There was only one blast, not two as previously reported," Farooq Abdullah told Reuters in New Delhi by telephone from Jammu, the state's winter capital. "We strongly condemn this attack. Innocent people have died. Terrorism must stop."
Earlier reports had said there were two blasts in the city's crowded central bus station and put the death toll at 15.
Abdullah said the bomb was planted in a Gypsy, an all-terrain vehicle.

"There were a lot of vehicles moving around. We don't know if the Gypsy was moving at the time. It destroyed a bus next to it. I have just come back from the hospital and a number of people have been injured by flying metal and glass. One man was very seriously injured."

The blast occurred on the second day of crucial talks between Indian and Pakistani diplomats in New Delhi. The bitter rivals have fought two wars since independence from Britain in 1947 over the Himalayan territory of Kashmir.

Asked if authorities had any clues as to who had planted the bomb, Abdullah said: "There are a number of people who do not want the talks to succeed. We are trying to determine the origin of the car bomb."
Kuldip Khuda, the Inspector-General of Police for the Jammu region, said "very sophisticated material" was used by the bomb-makers and forensic experts were sifting through the debris.
He told Reuters in Jammu that two other buses and some nearby shops were also damaged.

The bomb went off just as several senior Jammu and Kashmir officials were driving along a street on the other side of the bus station towards a nearby stadium to attend a concert. Police said none of the government officials was injured.
A police spokesman said the bomb exploded at about 6:40 p.m. (1310 GMT) near a tourist bus waiting to depart for Delhi, 500 km (300 miles) to the south.
Gyan Chand, whose older brother died in the blast, said he had just stepped away from the bus to make a telephone call. "There was a huge blast followed by a fire," he told Reuters.
Most of the injured were taken to the Government Medical College in the city, the predominantly Hindu winter capital of India's Moslem-majority Jammu and Kashmir state.
"I was in the adjacent bus when the blast went off. The entire area was engulfed in smoke and flames. I ran for my life," said Hans Raj, an injured survivor, speaking from a hospital bed.
There was chaos in the hospital as volunteers queued to donate blood and doctors rushed the seriously injured into operating theatres.

The last round of India-Pakistan talks collapsed in January 1994 over Kashmir, where a separatist Moslem revolt has been raging since 1980 in the part of the Himalayan region controlled by India. Pakistan rules one-third of Kashmir and India the rest.
More than 20,000 people have been killed in Kashmir since the start of an armed revolt there in January 1990.
Hindu migrants from Kashmir staged noisy protests in New Delhi on Saturday against last week's killings of seven members of their community by unidentified gunmen, witnesses said.

Twelve Hindu families left their homes in the Moslem-dominated Kashmir Valley on Friday and arrived in Jammu, where they told reporters they feared for their lives after the killings in Sangrampur, a village in Budgam district.
